newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish church plans beatification of martyr priest.
newsitem.headline: Polish church plans beatification of martyr priest.

text.p: Poland's Roman Catholic Church at the weekend opened beatification proceedings for Jerzy Popieluszko, a leading pro-Solidarity priest abducted, tortured and murdered by communist security police in 1984.

The primate of Poland, Cardinal Jozef Glemp, presided over a mass late on Saturday at the north Warsaw church of St Stanislaw Kostka, which became a bastion of anti-communist opposition when Popieluszko was one of its priests.
Earlier on Saturday a church tribunal, which will hear testimony on Popieluszko's life from some 60 witnesses, held its first sitting following more than a year of preparations.

The start of the process, drawing attention to a notorious crime under the pre-1989 communist system, falls months before Poland's ruling ex-communists face a challenge in parliamentary elections from a right-wing alliance grouped around the strongly pro-Church Solidarity union.
Church leaders said the beatification should not be used to stir up support for parties opposed to the ruling left.

"The church is concerned that this should be carried out in an honest, thorough manner, and that it should avoid populist and political elements," Zdzislaw Krol, the priest who is advocating the beatification, told Polish public television.
Despite such pledges, attitudes on religion are set to play a key part in campaigning for the polls, likely in September.
This is partly because the ex-communists late last year steered through a law liberalising Poland's anti-abortion rules, despite protests from the church and Pope John Paul ll.

The Pope is due to visit his native Poland for 11 days from May 31, partly to mark the 1,000th anniversary of the martyrdom of Poland's first patron saint, Wojciech (Adalbert), and the trip is likely to boost the opposition's morale.

A church spokesman in the western city of Gniezno, where Wojciech's remains lie, said the presidents of the Czech Republic, Germany, Poland, Slovakia and Hungary had agreed to attend ceremonies there on June 3, PAP news agency reported.

The ex-communists, who regrouped as social democrats after the 1989 collapse of the old system and went on to beat Solidarity-rooted parties in 1993 polls, on Saturday adopted a new draft programme underlining their secular standpoint.

"We will fight against intolerance and clericalism," their leader Jozef Oleksy told a national congress of the Social Democracy of the Republic of Poland, core party in the ruling Democratic Left Alliance, in Warsaw.
The programme condemned evils of the past system and crimes committed under Stalinism in the 1950s, but paid tribute to those who it said had worked honestly for Poland before 1989.
Popieluszko gained great popularity for his defiant sermons which continued following the 1981 martial-law crackdown on Solidarity by the then Communist leader Wojciech Jaruzelski.
The priest was badly beaten, then thrown bound and weighted by stones into a river. Jaruzelski put the four police officers who killed him on trial in 1985, and they were jailed.

Warsaw's appeal court last year set aside the acquittal of Communist-era generals Wladyslaw Ciaston and Zenon Platek on charges of instigating the murder and ruled that they should face further proceedings.
